Gradle Testing JVM Projects

This content was generated with the assistance of AI and should be verified against the official documentation before being relied on in production.

The reference material consulted while preparing these pages is listed in the section bibliography.

This page is written against Gradle 9.8.1 (the current release on 2026-10-16). Every example was run through the Gradle wrapper on macOS with JDK 26 (Oracle java version "26"), which is the JVM that runs the daemon and that compiles the code, apart from the one example that moves the tests to another JDK. The Kotlin DSL is shown first and the Groovy DSL second wherever the syntax differs, and the tidepool build was run in both DSLs with the same commands; the console output is the same apart from timings and from the order in which independent tasks are reported. Every example ran with the configuration cache on (org.gradle.configuration-cache=true in gradle.properties) and reported no configuration cache problems, so all of them are compatible with it (a run with --warning-mode all printed no deprecation warning for the build of this page). The scratch project pointed its wrapper at a local copy of the distribution archive; the properties file that a real project commits is

distributionBase=GRADLE_USER_HOME
distributionPath=wrapper/dists
distributionSha256Sum=dce76f55f8e251a3a1f130eb120f30b3d271de2b76c9b0729d316b5a1b6dc01f
distributionUrl=https\://services.gradle.org/distributions/gradle-9.8.1-bin.zip
networkTimeout=10000
retries=0
retryBackOffMs=500
validateDistributionUrl=true
zipStoreBase=GRADLE_USER_HOME
zipStorePath=wrapper/dists

In the listings the lines about the configuration cache (Calculating task graph ..., Reusing configuration cache., Configuration cache entry stored. and the like) are left out, and the project directory of the scratch copy is replaced by /work/tidepool. A line consisting of ... marks output that was cut. The JVM default locale on the machine was Spanish; the Checkstyle examples set org.gradle.jvmargs=-Duser.language=en -Duser.country=US in gradle.properties, because otherwise Checkstyle prints its messages in Spanish, and no other output on this page depends on the locale. Features newer than Gradle 8.14 name their release. Gradle 8.14 was not installed here, so what differs in it comes from the official documentation and release notes and is labelled "not run here".

Testing is where the three build tools differ least in what they do and most in how they are told to do it. All of them compile the test sources against the production classes, start a JVM, hand the test classes to a framework and turn the result into a report that CI servers can read. Ant has no idea what a test is until you call the <junit> or <junitlauncher> task (see Testing with JUnit & junitlauncher); Maven binds the Surefire plugin to the test phase and the Failsafe plugin to integration-test (see Maven Testing with Surefire and Maven Integration Testing with Failsafe). Gradle has a task type, Test, that every JVM plugin instantiates for you, plus a declarative layer on top of it, the JVM Test Suite plugin, that is the recommended way to describe more than one kind of test. This page is about both layers, about the test frameworks Gradle can drive, about the reports it writes and about the plugins that measure and police tests: JaCoCo for coverage, Checkstyle and PMD for static checks. The Java plugins whose source sets the tests live in are on Gradle Java Projects; choosing the JDK that runs the tests is on Gradle Toolchains; testing a Gradle plugin with TestKit is on Testing & Publishing Plugins. For the language-level view of testing see Java Testing, Kotlin Testing and Groovy Testing with Spock & Geb.

The pieces: source set, Test task, test suite

Three objects take part in every test run, and most of the confusion about Gradle testing comes from not keeping them apart.

Object What it is Where it comes from

Source set test

A directory tree (src/test/java, src/test/resources) and the compile task, classes directory and configurations (testImplementation, testRuntimeOnly, testCompileClasspath, testRuntimeClasspath) derived from its name.

The java plugin creates it. Its classpath contains the production classes, which is why tests can call main code without declaring a dependency.

Test task test

A task that starts a separate JVM (the test worker), loads the test classes in it, runs them with a test framework and writes the results. Its inputs are the test classes, the runtime classpath and its own settings; its outputs are the XML results and the HTML report.

Registered for each suite, so test for the default suite, integrationTest for a suite of that name, and so on.

Test suite test (type JvmTestSuite)

A named bundle of sources, dependencies, testing framework and one or more targets, each backed by a Test task.

The JVM Test Suite plugin, applied by the java plugin. It is the declarative front end of the two objects above.

Before 7.3 (2021) only the first two existed, and a second kind of tests meant a hand-made source set, configurations and a Test task, as shown on Gradle Java Projects. The JVM Test Suite plugin was introduced in Gradle 7.3 as an incubating feature and does the same in a few declarative lines. The java-test-fixtures plugin (Gradle 5.6) shares test helpers between projects, JUnit 5 support arrived in Gradle 4.6, and the sections below add what came later: richer HTML reports (9.3), non-class-based tests (9.4) and the changes of Gradle 9.0 that made the conventions of Test tasks explicit.

Source: Gradle User Manual: Testing in Java & JVM projects, JVM Test Suite plugin: terminology, Gradle 7.3 release notes, Gradle 5.6 release notes, Gradle 4.6 release notes

The example build

The running example is tidepool, the small tide prediction toolkit of the other pages of this section. For testing it has four subprojects: tidepool-model (records plus test fixtures), tidepool-engine (the TideEngine and a CSV StationReader, with three kinds of tests), tide-test-engine (a tiny JUnit Platform engine used in the section on non-class-based tests) and tidepool-reports (a project that only aggregates reports). The tree of the files that matter for testing, build output left out (the build.gradle.kts files are build.gradle in the Groovy DSL):

tidepool
|-- build.gradle.kts
|-- settings.gradle.kts
|-- gradle.properties
|-- gradle/libs.versions.toml
|-- data/stations.csv
|-- tidepool-model
|   |-- build.gradle.kts
|   `-- src
|       |-- main/java/io/tidepool/model/...
|       |-- test/java/io/tidepool/model/HeightTest.java
|       `-- testFixtures/java/io/tidepool/model/Stations.java
|-- tidepool-engine
|   |-- build.gradle.kts
|   `-- src
|       |-- main/java/io/tidepool/engine/{StationReader,TideEngine}.java
|       |-- test/java/io/tidepool/engine/{StationReaderTest,TideEngineTest}.java
|       |-- integrationTest/java/io/tidepool/engine/StationReaderIT.java
|       `-- goldenTest/definitions/{diurnal/K1.tide,semidiurnal/M2.tide}
|-- tide-test-engine
|   |-- build.gradle.kts
|   `-- src/main/{java/io/tidepool/testengine/TideTestEngine.java,resources/META-INF/services/...}
`-- tidepool-reports
    `-- build.gradle.kts

The settings file, the version catalog and gradle.properties are the same as on the other pages (repositories declared once, versions in the catalog), reduced to what this page needs:

Kotlin DSL: settings.gradle.kts
dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositoriesMode = RepositoriesMode.FAIL_ON_PROJECT_REPOS
    repositories {
        mavenCentral()
    }
}

rootProject.name = "tidepool"

include("tidepool-model", "tidepool-engine", "tide-test-engine", "tidepool-reports")
Groovy DSL: settings.gradle
dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositoriesMode = RepositoriesMode.FAIL_ON_PROJECT_REPOS
    repositories {
        mavenCentral()
    }
}

rootProject.name = 'tidepool'

include 'tidepool-model', 'tidepool-engine', 'tide-test-engine', 'tidepool-reports'
gradle.properties
org.gradle.configuration-cache=true
group=io.tidepool
version=1.0.0
gradle/libs.versions.toml (the same for both DSLs; highlight.js has no TOML grammar, so it is shown as plain text)
[versions]
commons-csv = "1.14.1"
junit = "6.1.3"

[libraries]
commons-csv = { module = "org.apache.commons:commons-csv", version.ref = "commons-csv" }
junit-platform-engine = { module = "org.junit.platform:junit-platform-engine" }
junit-bom = { module = "org.junit:junit-bom", version.ref = "junit" }

The tests themselves are plain JUnit Jupiter. The engine’s unit tests, in tidepool-engine/src/test/java/io/tidepool/engine/TideEngineTest.java, use a parameterized test and the Stations fixture of the model project:

package io.tidepool.engine;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertTrue;

import io.tidepool.model.Stations;
import java.time.Instant;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource;

class TideEngineTest {
    @Test
    void flatWaterStaysFlat() {
        assertEquals(0.0, TideEngine.predict(Stations.flatWater(), Instant.EPOCH).metres());
    }

    @Test
    void pureM2StartsAtItsAmplitude() {
        assertEquals(1.0, TideEngine.predict(Stations.pureM2(), Instant.EPOCH).metres(), 1e-9);
    }

    @ParameterizedTest(name = "t = {0} s")
    @ValueSource(longs = {0, 3_600, 21_600, 43_200, 86_400})
    void heightNeverExceedsTheAmplitude(long epochSecond) {
        double metres = TideEngine.predict(Stations.pureM2(), Instant.ofEpochSecond(epochSecond)).metres();
        assertTrue(Math.abs(metres) <= 1.0 + 1e-9, "height " + metres);
    }
}

StationReaderTest parses a text block of CSV and has one test tagged @Tag("slow") that parses 20,000 stations; HeightTest in the model project checks a record and the fixture. The whole project was built with ./gradlew check (after clean in the Kotlin DSL copy) and ended with BUILD SUCCESSFUL in both DSLs.

The Test task

A Test task does five things, and each is a place where a build can be configured or can go wrong.

  1. It resolves the test runtime classpath and the directories of compiled test classes (testClassesDirs). Both are properties of the task; for the test task of the java plugin they are wired to the test source set.

  2. It starts a JVM, the test worker (the console calls it Gradle Test Executor N), with the settings of the task: maxHeapSize, jvmArgs, systemProperty, environment, workingDir (the project directory by default), the javaLauncher (the JDK) and so on.

  3. In that JVM, the tests are detected by inspecting the compiled test classes, with criteria that depend on the framework: for JUnit 3 and 4 a class that inherits from TestCase, carries @RunWith or has an @Test method; for TestNG the methods annotated with @Test. scanForTestClasses = false switches the scan off so that only the include and exclude patterns select classes. With the JUnit Platform the scan setting has no effect: only include and exclude filter the classes, and the engines found on the classpath do the discovery. Abstract classes are not executed.

  4. It executes the tests and streams the events to the build, which prints them according to testLogging, writes the XML result files and the HTML report, and fails the task when a test failed (unless ignoreFailures is true).

  5. It records inputs and outputs, so that a second run with nothing changed is UP-TO-DATE.

The properties used most often:

Property or option Effect

useJUnitPlatform(), useJUnit(), useTestNG()

Selects the framework of a hand-made Test task. With the test suite DSL you use useJUnitJupiter(), useJUnit(), useTestNG() or useSpock() on the suite instead, which also adds the framework’s dependencies.

maxHeapSize, minHeapSize, jvmArgs, jvmArgumentProviders, enableAssertions

JVM settings of the worker. Assertions (-ea) are on by default.

systemProperty(name, value), systemProperties, environment(name, value), workingDir

Properties, environment variables and working directory of the worker. System properties of the Gradle process are not passed on, so only the ones set here reach the worker; environment variables are: the worker starts with the environment of the build process, and environment adds to it or overrides entries.

include, exclude, filter { ... }, --tests

Select which classes or methods run (see "Selecting tests" below).

maxParallelForks, forkEvery

How many worker JVMs run at the same time and after how many test classes a worker is replaced.

failFast, --fail-fast, ignoreFailures

Stop at the first failed test; let the build go on after failures.

failOnNoDiscoveredTests

Since Gradle 9.0, fail when there are test sources but no test was discovered (default true).

testLogging { ... }

What is printed to the console while the tests run.

reports { html, junitXml }, binaryResultsDirectory

Where and whether the HTML report and the XML result files are written.

javaLauncher

The JDK that runs the worker (a toolchain launcher).

testDefinitionDirs

Directories with non-class-based test definition files (incubating, Gradle 9.4).

dryRun, --test-dry-run

Incubating: report the tests without executing them.

The command line options of the task are listed by help --task:

./gradlew :tidepool-engine:help --task test

Options

     --no-debug-jvm     Disables option --debug-jvm.
     --fail-fast     Stops test execution after the first failed test.

     --test-dry-run     Simulate test execution.
     --no-test-dry-run     Disables option --test-dry-run.

8 actionable tasks: 8 executed

Two things in that listing are worth noticing. The test fixtures of the model project (compileTestFixturesJava, testFixturesJar) were built because the engine’s tests depend on them, and the engine’s test task ran after its inputs were ready without the build script ordering anything: task dependencies come from the dependencies of the classpath. A second run with nothing changed does not run the tests at all, which is the incremental build at work (see Incremental Build). The options --rerun (rerun this one task) and the task cleanTest (delete its outputs) force a run:

./gradlew --configuration-cache :tidepool-engine:test
./gradlew --configuration-cache :tidepool-engine:test --rerun
./gradlew --configuration-cache :tidepool-engine:cleanTest :tidepool-engine:test
> Task :tidepool-engine:test UP-TO-DATE
BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 730ms

> Task :tidepool-engine:test
BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 3s

> Task :tidepool-engine:cleanTest
> Task :tidepool-engine:test
BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 3s

(three separate runs; only the lines about the test task and the result are shown). --rerun applies to the one task it follows, unlike --rerun-tasks, which reruns every task of the build, compilation included. Do not make a Test task always run by switching up-to-date checking off (outputs.upToDateWhen { false }); use --rerun when you need it, because the build cache and the caching of the other tasks depend on the task being well behaved.

Source: Gradle User Manual: Test execution, Test detection, DSL reference: Test, Forcing tests to run, Debugging when running tests

The JUnit Platform and its launcher

Gradle runs JUnit 5 and 6 (JUnit Jupiter) on the JUnit Platform. Since Gradle 4.6 a Test task switches to the platform with useJUnitPlatform(). What the task needs on the test runtime classpath is more than the Jupiter API: it needs a Jupiter engine, and it needs the JUnit Platform launcher, which is the entry point that Gradle calls inside the worker. The launcher and the engines must have versions that belong together, which is why the JUnit team publishes a bill of materials (org.junit:junit-bom).

Older builds got the launcher for free: Gradle loaded some test framework classes from its own distribution. That behavior was deprecated in Gradle 8.x ("Relying on automatic test framework implementation dependencies", announced for removal in 9.0.0) because it caused version conflicts with the test classpath, and in Gradle 9 it is gone. A hand-written Test task therefore has to declare the launcher. The following engine build, which wires the framework by hand, shows what happens when it does not (the build was otherwise the same as the one above; this is a scratch variation):

Kotlin DSL: tidepool-engine/build.gradle.kts (scratch variation, wired by hand)
plugins {
    `java-library`
}

dependencies {
    api(project(":tidepool-model"))
    implementation(libs.commons.csv)
    testImplementation(testFixtures(project(":tidepool-model")))
    testImplementation(platform("org.junit:junit-bom:6.1.3"))
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter")
}

tasks.withType<JavaCompile>().configureEach {
    options.release = 21
}

tasks.test {
    useJUnitPlatform()
}
Groovy DSL: tidepool-engine/build.gradle (scratch variation, wired by hand)
plugins {
    id 'java-library'
}

dependencies {
    api project(':tidepool-model')
    implementation libs.commons.csv
    testImplementation testFixtures(project(':tidepool-model'))
    testImplementation platform('org.junit:junit-bom:6.1.3')
    testImplementation 'org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter'
}

tasks.withType(JavaCompile).configureEach {
    options.release = 21
}

tasks.test {
    useJUnitPlatform()
}
> Task :tidepool-engine:test FAILED

Gradle Test Executor 27 FAILED
    org.gradle.api.internal.tasks.testing.TestSuiteExecutionException at SuiteTestDefinitionProcessor.java:45
        Caused by: org.gradle.api.internal.tasks.testing.RequiresTestFrameworkTestDefinitionProcessor$TestFrameworkNotAvailableException at JUnitPlatformTestDefinitionProcessor.java:101

FAILURE: Build failed with an exception.

* What went wrong:
Execution failed for task ':tidepool-engine:test' (registered by plugin 'org.gradle.jvm-test-suite').
> Test process encountered an unexpected problem.
   > Could not start Gradle Test Executor 27.
      > Failed to load JUnit Platform.  Please ensure that all JUnit Platform dependencies are available on the test's runtime classpath, including the JUnit Platform launcher.

* Try:
> Check common problems https://docs.gradle.org/9.8.1/userguide/java_testing.html#sec:java_testing_troubleshooting.
